newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar - China crushing hampered by dry weather.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China crushing hampered by dry weather.

text.p: Sugar crushing in parts of southern China has been hampered by dry weather, limiting the cane's moisture content and making farmers reluctant to continue harvesting, a sugar factory source said on Wednesday.
"Crushing is not going very well," the source, based in the southern Chinese province of Guangxi, told Reuters by telephone.
Cane received by factories was too light and was being sold by farmers in fits and starts, which affected factory profits as well as the quality of sugar produced, he said.
"The farmers get less money for light cane and so they want to wait for the cane stems to get heavier," the source said.
Very light rainfall currently sprinkling Guangxi may improve the situation, he added.
Some sugar factories were running out of cash to pay farmers for cane, exacerbating the crushing industry's woes, sugar traders in Hong Kong said.
Difficulties in crushing had nudged up spot sugar prices by about 50 yuan ($6) to the 4,250-4,300 yuan ($512-518) per tonne level of mid-November, sources said.
Ex-factory sugar prices for mid-December to January delivery were being quoted at 3,900 yuan ($470) per tonne.

But traders expected Guangxi's cane crop to be healthy, with estimates of a 200,000-300,000 tonne increase over last year to about 2.5 million tonnes, compared to China's total output of between 5.9 million and 6.2 million tonnes.

An unusual price gap which made northern beet sugar more expensive than southern cane sugar had narrowed, cutting profits for domestic traders who were buying in the north and selling in the south, a senior sugar trader in Hong Kong said.
"Sugar in the north is now 4,000 yuan ($482) per tonne, compared to about 4,200 yuan ($506) in the south. But if you add the transport costs, there's no profit in moving sugar down," he said.

Premiums for Thai raw sugar for January/March delivery were steady this week after falls in global sugar prices brought on by small-scale buying interest from Chinese trade houses, Japanese traders said.
Premiums for January/March delivery were quoted at 0.80/0.90 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB basis, against 0.75/0.90 cents a week ago.
March/May and May/July deliveries were a tad easier, both quoted at 0.45/0.55 cents on the New York exchange, the traders said.
Japanese traders, who finished covering requirements for January and March shipments, have started to buy April and June delivery, but activity was slow on fears of a further price drop.
